title: A Grandmaster Plays a Beginner | Chess Mastery Explained

moves.spoken: You answer e4 with e5, the most popular reply there is, claiming your share of the centre.
They bring the knight to f3, attacking your pawn on e5.
The knight to c6 defends the pawn and develops at the same time — the standard answer.
They play the bishop to b5 — the Ruy Lopez, also called the Spanish Game. The bishop hits the knight that defends e5, so the pressure on your pawn is indirect.
You put the question to the bishop with a6: take on c6, or retreat.
They drop the bishop back to a4. Taking on c6 and then on e5 looks tempting for them, but it is not as good as it looks — you get the pawn back.
You develop the knight to f6 and eye their pawn on e4 — but with your kingside still at home, grabbing it is not the priority.
They defend e4 with the knight to c3. With your bishop undeveloped and your king uncastled, taking pawns would be careless anyway.
b5 chases the bishop off a4 and ends its pressure on your knight on c6.
The bishop retreats to b3. Now give each piece its most active square, not the first square that comes to mind — every square has strengths and weaknesses.
For this bishop that square is c5: it watches the centre and aims at f2, the weakest point in their camp — a knight to g4 later would add to it.
They castle, still ordinary development in this line. Your bishop on c8 would like g4, to pin their knight to the queen.
d6 opens the diagonal for that bishop. They could stop it with h3 — a move like that is called prophylaxis: stopping your opponent's idea before it arrives.
They play d3 instead.
So the bishop goes to g4, pinning their knight on f3 to their queen. Both your bishops now work: one aims down the diagonal at their king, the other pins.
They kick the bishop with h3. Taking the knight on f3 is tempting, but this bishop's job is to keep that knight pinned.
So the bishop drops back to h5 and keeps the pin.
They answer with a pin of their own — the bishop to g5 pins your knight on f6 to your queen.
Both sides are pinned, and the question is who breaks free first. You borrow their idea: h6 kicks the bishop.
The bishop drops back to h4, keeping the pin.
g5 kicks the bishop again and breaks the pin for good. It loosens the pawns in front of your own king — that is the price of breaking free, and it is worth weighing every time.
